Chapter 5: Expanding Executive Power and Navigating Political Opposition
As the worst of the Great Depression starts to fade, Franklin Delano Roosevelt finds himself facing a whole new set of challenges. The bold moves of the New Deal have completely reshaped American politics—but they’ve also sparked heated arguments about just how much power a president should have, and what role the government ought to play in people’s lives.
So, imagine this: Franklin’s now right at the center of a political storm, trying to balance progress with tradition, and innovation with caution. One of the biggest debates swirling around him is about how far the federal government should go in regulating the economy and supporting its citizens. Franklin truly believes that desperate times call for bold action. But not everyone’s on board with that idea. Critics in Congress, the courts, and especially the business world, push back—claiming the New Deal is a massive overreach, threatening the balance of power and the core principles of limited government.
Things really come to a head with the Supreme Court. The justices strike down several key New Deal programs, calling them unconstitutional. For Franklin, this isn’t just a legal roadblock—it feels like a direct challenge to the very heart of democracy. So what does he do? True to form, he answers with boldness. He proposes expanding the number of Supreme Court justices—a controversial move that sets off a nationwide debate about separation of powers, executive overreach, and the future of American democracy itself.
This whole episode becomes a turning point. Franklin’s plan doesn’t pass. But it sends a strong message: he’s willing to fight for his vision of government, no matter the risk. And interestingly, even though his proposal fails, it nudges the Court to be more open to New Deal reforms moving forward. The takeaway? Sometimes, leadership means taking real risks—pushing boundaries, standing up for your beliefs, and learning from both wins and setbacks.
Throughout it all, Franklin keeps relying on his greatest strengths as a communicator and coalition-builder. He knows change isn’t just about big ideas—it’s about bringing people together. So he reaches out to labor leaders, business executives, and everyday Americans, searching for common ground and building alliances. The process isn’t always smooth. It’s messy, it’s noisy, but it’s the very heart of how democracy works.
And it’s not just outside opposition he has to handle. Franklin faces growing pushback from within his own party. Some think he’s gone too far, others argue he hasn’t gone far enough. The political landscape is fractured, and Franklin has to walk a careful line between all these competing interests. But through it all, he keeps his eyes on the bigger goal: building a society that’s fairer, more just, and more resilient.
Expanding executive power during this period is both a source of strength and a real cause for concern. Franklin gets that unchecked authority can be dangerous. But he also believes that the times demand decisive action. He’s careful to frame his choices around democratic values and the public good, always stressing the importance of accountability and transparency.
As the nation edges closer to World War II, the stakes only get higher. The lessons of the New Deal—the need for adaptability, the power of communication, and the courage to lead boldly—are about to be tested on a global stage. For now, Franklin’s legacy is one of transformation. He’s redefined what’s possible in American government, expanded the limits of presidential power, and shown just how valuable resilience and vision are when the world is in crisis.
